questions.question: In a periodic-review single-item inventory system with a constant lead time of $l\geq1$ periods and period demands $D_1,D_2,\ldots$, what does the lead-time demand $X$ measure?
options: The total demand between two consecutive order placements, over one order cycle.
The demand in the single period in which an outstanding order finally arrives.
The total demand of the $l$ periods during which a newly placed order is on its way.
The amount ordered at the start of a period to cover the demand of the next $l$ periods.

questions.question: A periodic-review inventory system has iid period demands $D_1,D_2,\ldots$ and lead time $l=0$, so orders arrive at once. What is the lead-time demand $X=\sum_{i=1}^{l}D_i$?
options: $X=0$ with certainty, since no demand occurs while an order is in transit.
$X=D_1$, since one period of demand still passes before the order arrives.
$X$ is undefined, since a sum running from $i=1$ to $0$ has no terms.
$X$ equals that period's order size, since this order arrives immediately.

questions.question: With lead time $l\geq1$, an order placed at the start of period $k-l$ arrives at the start of period $k$. Which sum is the demand that occurs while this order is in transit?
options: $D_{k-l}+D_{k-l+1}+\cdots+D_{k}$

questions.question: Period demands $D_1,\ldots,D_l$ each have finite mean $\mathbb{E}[D]$, and $X=D_1+\cdots+D_l$. Which assumption does $\mathbb{E}[X]=l\,\mathbb{E}[D]$ require?
options: Independence of the $D_i$, since expectations of a sum add only for independent terms.
Nothing beyond each $D_i$ having mean $\mathbb{E}[D]$, as linearity of expectation suffices.
Identical distributions of the $D_i$, since equal means alone do not fix $\mathbb{E}[X]$.
Nonnegative integer demands, so that $\mathbb{E}[X]$ can be found from a convolution.

questions.question: Period demands $D_1,D_2,\ldots$ are iid and the lead time is $l\geq1$. Why is the window sum $D_{k-l}+\cdots+D_{k-1}$ said to have the distribution of $X$ only for $k\geq l+1$?
options: For $k\leq l$ the demands are not yet identically distributed while the system starts up.
For $k\leq l$ the window holds more than $l$ demands, because period $k$ is also counted.
For $k\leq l$ the window would start before period $1$, so it has fewer than $l$ demands.
The window needs $l+1$ demands, and these first exist from period $k=l+1$ onwards.

questions.question: Iid period demands have mean $\mathbb{E}[D]=3$ units and the lead time is $l=4$ periods. What is the expected lead-time demand $\mathbb{E}[X]$?
Iid period demands have standard deviation $1.5$ units and the lead time is $l=4$ periods. What is the standard deviation of the lead-time demand $X$?
Iid period demands take values in $\{0,1,2,3,4\}$ with $\mathbb{P}(D=4)>0$, and the lead time is $l=3$. What is the smallest integer $x$ with $G_X(x)=\mathbb{P}(X>x)=0$?
Iid period demands take values in $\{0,1,2,3\}$ with $\mathbb{P}(D=3)=0.1$, and the lead time is $l=3$. What is $\mathbb{P}(X=9)$ for the lead-time demand $X$?

A deterministic EOQ system has demand rate $30$ units per week, order quantity $150$ units (a $5$-week cycle) and a lead time of $2$ weeks. At what on-hand stock level should an order be placed so that it arrives as stock runs out?
options: $30$ units
$60$ units
$90$ units
$150$ units

questions.question: With lead time $l\geq2$ and iid period demands with $\operatorname{Var}(D)>0$, a planner models the lead-time demand as $l D_1$ instead of $X=D_1+\cdots+D_l$. How do the two compare?
options: Same mean, but $lD_1$ has the larger variance: $l^2$ rather than $l$ times $\operatorname{Var}(D)$.
Same distribution, because $D_1,\ldots,D_l$ are all identically distributed.
Same mean and same variance $l\operatorname{Var}(D)$, because variances add over periods.
Same mean, but $X$ has the larger variance, because it adds $l$ random terms.

questions.question: Iid period demands are nonnegative integers, $X_l$ is the lead-time demand for lead time $l$, and $S$ is a fixed integer. How does $\mathbb{P}(X_{l+1}>S)$ compare with $\mathbb{P}(X_l>S)$ for every demand distribution?
options: It is always strictly larger, because one more period of demand is added.
It can be smaller, because the relative spread of $X_l$ shrinks as $l$ grows.
It can differ only if $S<l\,\mathbb{E}[D]$, that is, below the mean lead-time demand.
It is never smaller, since $X_{l+1}\geq X_l$; it can stay equal for some demands.

questions.question: Period demands $D_1,\ldots,D_l$ are iid with pmf $f_D$ and $l\geq2$. Which statement correctly gives the pmf $f_X$ of $X=D_1+\cdots+D_l$ and the property the derivation uses?
options: $f_X$ is the $l$-fold convolution of $f_D$; identical distributions suffice and independence is not used.
$f_X(x)=f_D(x)^l$ for every $x$; this uses that the $D_i$ are independent.
$f_X$ is the $l$-fold convolution of $f_D$; this uses that the $D_i$ are independent.
$f_X(x)=f_D(x/l)$ for every $x$; this uses that the $D_i$ are identically distributed.

questions.question: Iid period demands have pmf $\mathbb{P}(D=0)=0.3$, $\mathbb{P}(D=1)=0.5$, $\mathbb{P}(D=2)=0.2$, and the lead time is $l=2$. What is $\mathbb{P}(X=2)$ for $X=D_1+D_2$?
Iid period demands are nonnegative integers with $\mathbb{E}[D]=2.5$, and the lead time is $l=2$. With survivor function $G_X(j)=\mathbb{P}(X>j)$, what is $\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}G_X(j)$?

A base-stock policy has $S=3$, lead time $l=2$ and iid demands with $\mathbb{P}(D=0)=0.5$, $\mathbb{P}(D=1)=0.3$, $\mathbb{P}(D=2)=0.2$; the inventory level is distributed as $I=S-X$. What is $\mathbb{P}(I<0)$?

A deterministic EOQ system has demand rate $d$, order quantity $Q$, cycle length $T=Q/d$ and lead time $l$ with $T<l<2T$. Which reorder rule, using on-hand stock or the inventory position (on hand plus on order), makes every order arrive exactly when stock runs out?
options: Order when on-hand stock alone falls to $dl$, ignoring any order in transit.
Order when the inventory position falls to the lead-time demand $dl$.
Order when the position falls to $dl-Q$, one lot below the lead-time demand.
Order when the position covers a lead time plus a cycle, i.e. falls to $d(l+T)$.

questions.question: Period demands $D_1,D_2,\ldots$ are iid with $\operatorname{Var}(D)>0$ and the lead time is $l=3$. Let $W_4=D_1+D_2+D_3$ and $W_5=D_2+D_3+D_4$. Which statement about $W_4$ and $W_5$ is correct?
options: They are independent copies of $X$, because the demands are iid.
They are dependent, so $W_4$ has the distribution of $X$ but $W_5$ does not.
They are independent, but $W_5$ has the larger mean as it ends a period later.
Both have the distribution of $X$, but they are dependent as they share $D_2$ and $D_3$.

questions.question: Period demands are iid $\operatorname{Pois}(0.5)$ and the lead time is $l=4$ periods. What is $\mathbb{P}(X=2)$ for the lead-time demand $X=D_1+\cdots+D_4$?
options: $2\mathrm{e}^{-2}\approx0.271$
$\tfrac{1}{8}\mathrm{e}^{-0.5}\approx0.076$
$4\mathrm{e}^{-2}\approx0.541$

questions.question: Iid period demands have $\mathbb{E}[D]=2$ and $\operatorname{Var}(D)=1$. The lead time $L$ is independent of demand, with $L=1$ or $L=3$ each with probability $\tfrac{1}{2}$. What is $\operatorname{Var}(X)$ for $X=D_1+\cdots+D_L$?
